'''Audrey Doris Jones''' {{Post-nominals|size=100%|country=GBR|CPhys|FInstP}} ({{Nee|'''Stuckes'''}} {{IPAc-en|audio=En-uk-Stuckes.oga|s|t|uː|k|s}}; 15 September 1923{{Spaced ndash}}26 September 2006) was an English [[Materials science|material scientist]] and a senior lecturer in the department of [[Salford Acoustics|applied acoustics]] at the [[University of Salford]]. She made important contributions to the theory of the [[Johnsen–Rahbek effect]], the electrical and [[thermal conductivity and resistivity|thermal conductivity]] of [[semiconductor]]s, and the [[Thermal conductance and resistance|thermal resistance]] of building insulation. She was the only daughter of Frederick Stuckes, the general manager of a [[shipbroking]] firm, and was educated at [[Montpelier High School, Bristol|Colston's Girls' School]] in [[Bristol]]. In 1942, she won a scholarship to study the [[Natural Science Tripos]] at [[Newnham College, Cambridge|Newnham College]] in the [[University of Cambridge]].

Stuckes graduated in 1946 with a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] degree and joined [[Metropolitan-Vickers]], [[Trafford]], as a graduate trainee in the research department. From 1953, she published a series of papers on the thermal and electrical conductivity of semiconductors. She proved the existence of the Johnsen{{Nbh}}Rahbek effect and proposed an [[Electrical network|electric circuit]] model to explain the data. In December 1962, she was elected a Fellow of the Institute of Physics, and in the following year, she left Metropolitan{{Hyphen}}Vickers to work as a lecturer in the department of pure and applied physics at the Royal College of Advanced Technology, Salford, that became the University of Salford in 1967.

In 1975, Stuckes, together with John Edwin Parrott, published a well{{Hyphen}}received textbook that reviewed the theory and experimental data on thermal conductivity in solids and semiconductors. By 1979, she was a senior lecturer in the department of applied acoustics at Salford, and in the following year, she was in charge of the department's heat laboratory. The laboratory was supported by grants from, amongst others, the [[Science and Engineering Research Council]] and the [[Building Research Establishment]]. These grants funded studies to investigate the efficiency of insulating materials. She led a team to obtain experimental data that would allow builders to calculate a standard level of insulation. In 1982, she presented a television programme for the [[Open University]] that demonstrated the usefulness of these simple models of thermal conduction. She retired from the university in September 1988 and died after a long illness at a nursing home in [[Urmston]], Trafford.
{{TOC limit|2}}

== Early life ==
Stuckes was born on 15{{Nbsp}}September 1923 at [[Bristol]], England, the only daughter of Frederick Stephen Stuckes and Beatrice May, {{Nee|Cogan}}.{{R|"Clifton Society 13 January 1916"|"Western Daily Press 29 October 1947"}} They had married on 8{{Nbsp}}January 1916 at St{{Nbsp}}John the Baptist, [[Bedminster, Bristol|Bedminster]], Bristol.{{R|"Clifton Society 13 January 1916"}} Her father worked for Bethell, Gwyn, and Company (Bethell Gwyn), at 11{{Nbsp}}Baldwin Street, Bristol,{{R|"Arrowsmith 1915"}} a [[shipbroking]] firm dealing mainly with [[Australasia]]n trade.{{R|"Western Daily Press 27 December 1945"}} During [[World War I]], he [[Volunteer Force|volunteered]] as a [[Sergeant#United Kingdom|sergeant]] in the [[City of Bristol Rifles#1/4th (City of Bristol) Battalion|1/4th Battalion of the City of Bristol Rifles]],{{R|"Clifton Society 13 January 1916"}} and on 27{{Nbsp}}June 1917, he was commissioned a [[Second lieutenant#United Kingdom and other Commonwealth countries|second lieutenant]] in the [[Royal Warwickshire Regiment]].{{R|"London Gazette 13 July 1917"}} However, later that year, he was severely injured in a shell [[Barrage (artillery)|barrage]],{{R|"Bristol Evening Post 7 July 1956"}} and subsequently, he relinquished his commission on 22{{Nbsp}}June 1918.{{R|"London Gazette 18 June 1918"}}

After the war, Stuckes' father returned to Bethell Gwyn, and in March 1953, he was elected president of the Bristol Steamship Owners' Association.{{R|"Duff 1953a"}} He had been elected a fellow of the [[Institute of Chartered Shipbrokers]] in 1945,{{R|"Western Daily Press 27 December 1945"}} and in August 1953, he was elected chair of the Bristol section of the institute.{{R|"Duff 1953b"}} In September 1956, he retired from Bethell Gwyn after forty{{Hyphen}}eight years of service.{{R|"Wendon 1956"}}

== Education ==
[[File:Colston's Girls' School in 2009 (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright=0.85|alt=Colour photograph of the Grade II listed school building at Cheltenham Road, Montpelier, Bristol. The building is constructed from red bricks, with yellow brick and terracotta dressings, and a slate roof. The building is shown with three storeys and fourteen windows, facing a road with trees obscuring the view in the foreground.|[[Montpelier High School, Bristol|Colston's Girls' School]], Bristol, where Stuckes was educated]]
Stuckes was first educated at Merrywood primary school in Knowle, Bristol.{{R|"Western Daily Press 13 October 1933"}} In June 1934, she gained a foundational boarding scholarship to [[Redmaids' High School|Red Maids' School]], [[Westbury-on-Trym]].{{R|"Western Daily Press 2 June 1934"}} She went on to study at [[Montpelier High School, Bristol|Colston's Girls' School]], [[Ashley (Bristol ward)#Montpelier|Montpelier]], Bristol, where, in July 1942, she passed her [[Higher School Certificate (England and Wales)|Higher School Certificate]] in [[natural science]]s with a distinction in chemistry.{{R|"Western Daily Press 1 August 1942"}} She was offered a [[Emily Jane Pfeiffer|Pfeiffer]] scholarship at [[Bedford College, London|Bedford College]], [[University of London]], and awarded a Gamble scholarship by the school of £50 a year ({{Inflation|UK|50|1942|fmt=eq|r=-2|cursign=£}}),{{R|"Western Daily Press 27 November 1945"}} that was tenable at the universities of Oxford, Cambridge, London, and at the [[London School of Medicine for Women#History|Royal Free Hospital for Women]].{{R|"Burrow's Scholastic Bureau 1958"}}{{Efn|The scholarship was granted in years when the [[Catherine Winkworth]] scholarship was not available.{{R|"Burrow's Scholastic Bureau 1958"}}}}

However, instead of taking up the scholarship at Bedford, Stuckes entered [[Newnham College, Cambridge|Newnham College]] in the [[University of Cambridge]],{{R|"Western Daily Press 1 April 1942"}} to study the [[Natural Science Tripos]].{{R|"Cambridge University Calendar Supplement 1944"}} In 1946, she graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] degree,{{R|"Cambridge University List of Members 2000"}} and in the same year, she was elected a student member of the [[Physical Society of London]].{{R|"Proceedings of the Physical Society 1946"}} In 1950, she was elected an associate of the [[Institute of Physics]] and awarded an [[Master of Arts#Oxford, Cambridge, Dublin (conferred)|MA]] by Cambridge.{{R|"Physics Bulletin 1950"|p=6}} In 1969, she returned to Cambridge to complete a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]], and subsequently, she was elected to the [[Academic senate|senate]] of the university.{{R|"Cambridge University List of Members 2000"}}

== Career ==
{{Hatnote|See {{Section link||Selected publications}} for details of Stuckes' academic papers}}
[[File:William Waldegrave visiting the acoustic department at the University of Salford in 1981.jpg|thumb|alt=Monochrome photograph of William Waldegrave's visit to the heat laboratory at the University of Salford in 1981. Waldegrave is shown stood with Stuckes, the then head of the laboratory, and John Ashworth. They are photographed behind a table holding anechoic poly blocks.|Stuckes meeting [[William Waldegrave, Baron Waldegrave of North Hill|William Waldegrave]] (left) and [[Chancellor (education)#Vice-chancellor|vice-chancellor]] [[John Ashworth (biologist)|John Ashworth]] (right), at the [[University of Salford]]'s heat laboratory in 1981]]
After leaving Cambridge, Stuckes joined [[Metropolitan-Vickers]], [[Trafford]], Greater Manchester, as a graduate trainee in the research department.{{Sfn|Stuckes|1953|p=570}} Metropolitan{{Hyphen}}Vickers was a British heavy industrial firm, known for manufacturing electrical equipment and generators, street lighting, and electronics.{{R|"Grace's Guide 2022"}} The company had a relatively favourable attitude to placing graduate women in professional electrical engineering positions. For example, when Stuckes joined the company, [[Beryl May Dent|Beryl Dent]] led the computation section and supervised the laboratory team that investigated the physical properties of [[semiconductor]]s.{{R|1="Black Muddiman Plant 2007"|p1=232|2="Dent 1957"|p2=11}} Stuckes collaborated with Dent on Stuckes' first published paper on the heating effects that occur when a current is passed through a semiconductor.{{Sfn|Stuckes|1953|p=570}} Dent suggested methods to solve the equations and computed the [[numerical integration]]s.{{Sfn|Stuckes|1953|p=587}}

From 1953, Stuckes published a series of papers on the thermal and electrical conductivity of semiconductors. In one such paper, she investigated the [[Electrostatics|electrostatic]] force between polished plates of a semiconductor and a metal when placed in contact and a voltage applied.{{R|"Sawyer 1957"|p=183}} The force is caused by the [[Polarization density|free charge]] that accumulates between the semiconductor and metal surfaces.{{R|"Wang Lu Cheng 2019"}} This force, or attraction, is known as the [[Johnsen–Rahbek effect]], and is proportional to the square of the applied voltage.{{R|"Holm 1981"|pp=59{{Ndash}}60}} Stuckes constructed a [[clutch]] that consisted of a plate of [[Titanate#Orthotitanates|magnesium orthotitanate]], a hard, ceramic semiconductor, that rubbed against a highly{{Hyphen}}polished steel plate.{{R|"Levermore 1975"|p=12}} She found that abrasion at the contact surfaces caused the force to decrease as the number of operations increased and suggested the presence of an [[Field electron emission|electron field emission]] effect at the contact boundary.{{R|1="Holm 1981"|pp1=59{{Ndash}}60|2="Rajagopalan Muthu Liu 2022"|p2=5}} She proved the existence of the effect, proposed an [[Electrical network|electric circuit]] model to explain the data,{{R|"Shultz Peshkin Colgate 2015"|p=59}} and noted that as the voltage increased, the area of field emission also increased, and consequently, this limited the [[field strength]] of the circuit.{{R|"Rajagopalan Muthu Liu 2022"|p=5}}

On 4{{Nbsp}}December 1962, Stuckes was elected a [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics]],{{R|"Physics Bulletin 1963"|p=22}} and in the subsequent year, she left Metropolitan{{Hyphen}}Vickers to work as a lecturer in the department of pure and [[applied physics]] at the Royal College of Advanced Technology, Salford,{{Sfn|Stuckes|Farrell|1964|p=477}} that became the [[University of Salford]] in 1967.{{R|"Gordon 1975"|p=198}} In 1975, Stuckes, together with John Edwin Parrott, published a [[textbook]] that reviewed the theory and experimental data on thermal conductivity in solids and semiconductors. Parrott was a scientist at the [[Aldermaston Court]] research laboratory of [[Associated Electrical Industries]] (the then [[holding company]] of Metropolitan{{Hyphen}}Vickers), and later, professor of physics at [[University of Wales]], [[Cardiff]].{{R|"Karpeta 1991"}} In 1956, he had obtained a PhD from the [[University of Reading]] on the thermal and thermoelectric properties of semiconductors.{{R|"Parrott 1956"}} Paul Gustav Klemens, late professor of physics at the [[University of Connecticut]],{{R|"Pohl 2012"}} reviewed the book at the time of publication and stated that "[it] is most unique and valuable; the theoretical problem is very difficult, and nowhere is there such a good summary of the useful approximations and the salient results."{{R|"Klemens 1977"|p=61}}

{{Quote box
| quote = The builder is putting the material in an environment that is different from the one in which the conductivity has been measured.
| author = Stuckes
| source = {{Citeref|Kenward|1980|7 February 1980|style=plain}} edition of the ''[[New Scientist]]''
| width = 20%
| bgcolor = AliceBlue
| qalign = left
| align = right
}}
By 1979, Stuckes was a senior lecturer in the [[Salford Acoustics|department of applied acoustics]] at Salford,{{R|"Stewart 1979"}} and in 1980, she was in charge of the department's heat laboratory.{{R|"Physics Bulletin 1981"}} The laboratory was supported by grants from the Polymer Engineering Directorate and the Building Subcommittee (she was a member of this committee in 1982){{R|"SERC 1982"}} of the [[Science and Engineering Research Council]],{{R|"The Times Higher Education Supplement 25 January 1980"}} and the [[Building Research Establishment]] in the [[Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions|Department of the Environment]].{{R|"Physics Bulletin 1981"}} These grants funded a study to investigate how moisture in [[cavity wall]]s affects the surrounding insulation.{{R|"Kenward 1980"}} At the time, no one knew the exact efficiency of standard [[polymer]]ic insulating materials as data was based on material in "dry" condition. Stuckes led a team to obtain experimental data that would allow builders to calculate a standard level of insulation.{{R|"Kenward 1980"}} The study concluded that heat transfer in buildings can be modelled adequately by simple, one{{Hyphen}}dimensional, [[steady state]] models.{{R|"Fendrich 1994"}}

In 1981, Stuckes was interviewed by [[Alfred Bates]] about the most efficient way to heat and insulate homes. The interview was broadcast on 31{{Nbsp}}March 1981, as part of a [[BBC North West]] regional [[television documentary]] series entitled ''Towards Tomorrow''.{{R|"The Bolton News 31 March 1981"}} In the following year, she presented a television programme for the [[Open University]] that demonstrated the usefulness of simple models of [[thermal conduction]].{{R|"Fendrich 1994"}}{{Efn|See [[#External links|One{{Hyphen}}dimensional steady state heat transfer]] in the external links section for a video of the Open University programme presented by Stuckes.}} The programme was first broadcast on [[BBC One]] in the morning of 3{{Nbsp}}May 1982 and formed part of the Open University's [[Course credit|unit]] on heat transfer.{{R|"Radio Times 1982"|"Open University 1982"}} In the 1980s, she continued to publish research on the thermal properties of building materials. In one study with Anthony Simpson,{{Efn|Prior to 2025, Simpson was head of the thermal laboratory at Salford.{{R|"Simpson 2024"}}}} they found that the shape of air [[Inclusion (mineral)|inclusion]]s within [[Vermiculite#Roof and floor screeds and insulating concretes|vermiculite concrete]] affected the thermal conductivity of the concrete.{{Sfn|Simpson|Stuckes|1987|p=4}} This finding was explored further with [[BP|British Petroleum]] and resulted in a joint [[patent]] being granted on a thermally insulating [[Filler (materials)|filler]].{{Sfn|Simpson|Stuckes|1984}} By May 1986, she was awarded [[Chartered Physicist]] status by the Institute of Physics,{{Sfn|Simpson|Stuckes|1986|p=78}} and by September 1988, she had retired from her position at the university.{{Sfn|Simpson|Stuckes|Napora|1988|p=159}}

== Personal life and death ==
In retirement, Stuckes resided at 58 Carlton Road in [[Hale, Greater Manchester|Hale]], Trafford.{{R|"Directory of British Scientists 1964"}} In October 1947, she had become engaged to Douglas Perrin Jones, the eldest son of William Henry Perrin Jones of [[Port Sunlight]], [[Metropolitan Borough of Wirral|Wirral]].{{R|"Western Daily Press 29 October 1947"}} At the time of their engagement, Douglas was an electrical engineer in the research department at Metropolitan{{Hyphen}}Vickers.{{R|"Brownlee Mitchell 1952"|p=716}} When they both worked there, he would assist in her research, including in 1953, an investigation into the heating effects that occur when a current is passed through a semiconductor.{{Sfn|Stuckes|1953|p=587}} After their marriage at Bristol in 1949,{{R|"Geer 2022"}} she continued to use her maiden name in her academic life and scientific publications.{{R|"Directory of British Scientists 1964"}}

Douglas retired in 1984 after 46 years' service as a research engineer with the [[General Electric Company]]. He died in hospital on 15{{Nbsp}}July 1995, aged 75 years, and his funeral service was held on 21{{Nbsp}}July 1995 at Altrincham Crematorium, [[Dunham Massey]].{{R|"Manchester Evening News 18 July 1995"}} Stuckes died after a long illness on 26{{Nbsp}}September 2006, aged 83 years,{{R|"The Daily Telegraph 10 October 2006"}} at Faversham Nursing Home, [[Urmston]], Trafford.{{R|"Altrincham Crematorium 2006"}} Her funeral service was held at the same crematorium on 3{{Nbsp}}October 2006 and her ashes were later interred in the crematorium grounds.{{R|"The Daily Telegraph 10 October 2006"}}
